pure-announcement.rationale: It is an analysis of study findings, not a launch, release or funding announcement.

duplicate.rationale: None of the nearest existing concepts (shared-mental-model-erosion, multi-agent-token-economics, siem-agentic-visibility-gap, tail-latency-histograms, agent-outcome-vs-proxy-metrics, agent-loop-governance) cover breach-cost drivers.

unfalsifiable.rationale: Claims are attributed to a named, reproducible annual methodology (IBM/Ponemon Institute, 524 breaches studied) even though this hunt could not independently re-verify the raw figures.

durability.rationale: Even IBM's own analysis of its own study is carried almost entirely by single-study-year dollar figures and percentages (USD 2.45M vs 6.03M, a 200-day threshold, 61% first-year cost accrual, 19% cloud-misconfiguration share) drawn from the 2020 edition specifically, already six years stale and superseded by every later edition of the same report — the same problem the original source had, not solved by moving to IBM's own analysis of its own data.

actionability.rationale: It does name concrete, non-obvious levers a security budget-holder could act on: invest in security automation and a trained/tested incident-response team specifically because they shorten detection-to-containment time, and budget for breach costs across multiple years rather than assuming they land in year one.

atomicity.rationale: It bundles several distinct claims (automation's cost impact, incident-response-team readiness, breach-lifecycle length, multi-year cost accrual varying by industry regulation, cloud misconfiguration as a breach cause) under one 'factors in cost' umbrella without reducing to a single independent paragraph.
